children.author: gf000
children.text:
> Proton can’t change the fundamental nature of IMAP or SMTP

As the sibling commenter mentioned, exactly.

Since it can't be done securely, it is misleading and scammy to claim you somehow managed to secure something fundamentally impossible.

If you want secure communication, use a secure channel, like signal.

Proton can’t change the fundamental nature of IMAP or SMTP (and still be an “email” service. Their MTA must be able to read certain fields in the plain text email header; this doesn’t even change with PGP encrypted mail. Most MTAs use TLS for transport security. That prevents eavesdropping in transit. If you want maximal privacy from Proton, then you have the option of using PGP which introduces very high bars to working with others over email- you have to exchange keys out of band in a secure fashion, and then the other party has to either use a PGP-enabled mailer or has to know hotel to encrypt and decrypt.

Proton claims that their MTAs store the messages encrypted with a key for which they don’t possess the decryption key. This doesn’t seem like an unreasonable claim; this is a very well established pattern.

There is a window of time where for some messages they possess the plaintext of the message body that arrived at the MTA, and they make claims (I haven’t checked recently but was an early adopter and read them thoroughly when I first subscribed) that they don’t use that plaintext for business purposes and that they eliminate it from memory as fast as possible. Since I am not trying to defend myself against nation states, I’m willing to accept terms of service and implied contract as risk mitigation there.

If I capture the attention of Law Enforcement, then they can theoretically obtain orders to hand over logs, stored data, encryption keys, or (depending on jurisdiction), install or reconfigure systems to intercept plaintext prior to encryption. For this, I chose Proton because I live in the USA and my law enforcement agencies can’t skirt our fourth amendment with national security letters etc- they MUST obtain a warrant and they MUST work cooperatively with the law enforcement authorities in another country. I don’t think that in the reality we live in, that I as an individual would it’s only the resources of an individual can still use email in daily life and get any higher level of assurance. Anything else is fantasy.

I’m worried about protons business pricing- they are already outrageously expensive and getting more so and they are building AI dreck that I don’t care about; I just want secure email.

It seems obvious?

Proton reads all incoming email from non-Proton addresses, before message is encrypted with what they call Zero-access encryption. Zero access then seems more like a marketing gimmick, since technically, Proton has already accessed the contents at least once?

Quoted from their website:

... when an email is sent from Gmail to Proton Mail, Proton’s servers can briefly read the message ... Proton then encrypts the email using the recipient’s public key, after which only the recipient can decrypt it and Proton no longer has access.

https://proton.me/learn/encryption/types-of-encryption/zero-...

So you ge a somewhat false sense of privacy for emails at large . All those password reset emails from various devices, emails from anyone not on Proton etc... all accessible by Proton. Optimistically to protect you.

Meanwhile, if you lose your Proton recovery phrase you're potentially locked out of all those emails forever...

I’d like to see your evidence that “the only one from reading your email is yourself”.

I have fallen out of love with Proton the company, but ProtonMail does seem to fulfill its promise of encryption of incoming email at the MTA and storing only the cipher text. And their jurisdiction means that would be snoops in government agencies have to get cross-international-boundary data warrants (if you’re not Swiss). This seems to me like a very reasonable trade between privacy and ability of government to investigate crimes.

They have well integrated PGP support; it’s not their fault that no one uses it.

If you turn on any of their indexing stuff then yeah, all bets are off.

Hate on their business practices, sure, but if you’re going to attack their tech stack then back it up with facts and explain how anyone could do it better.

I used to be a paying customer, but encrypted email is a scam, the only one prevented from reading your emails is you yourself.

And this is quite literally true, I discontinued my subscription and.. email forwarding is paid, proton bridge is paid. There is literally no way to escape without paying, my proton email is basically hijacked.

As another tip, only use your own domain for emails, as it's not something you can just change later on.

children.text:
I'm not too interested in debating what should be considered a bug, but it doesn't seem to make sense to use IMAP in that way

Their documentation before the fix stated that "Paperless keeps track of emails it has processed in order to avoid processing the same mail multiple times. This uses the message UID provided by the mail server, which should be unique for each message." (https://web.archive.org/web/20260227170952/https://docs.pape...).

I think it's reasonable for a user to understand processing as in not downloading, either... (especially when it uses IMAP)

Nice how they called this "de-duplicating" by the way, in https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/pull/13432 .......

It's especially bad for a product meant to be hosted on a server, where you're very unlikely to notice huge unexpected traffic (and where you're going to have a fast connection).

It technically isn't a bug, but doesn't mean its not an issue.

It is abusive, I don't think you could hit someone and say "maybe you can't handle being punched is your problem".

I think they are wrong with how their thought process is, you shouldn't have to provide a mailbox for them to completely control... in that area we'd expect to push mail to the server instead. Maybe they shouldn't support IMAP then.

https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/issues/13175 , crazy, and they failed to see it as a bug?

I've been leaving almost all my mail as unread for decades, but I've never seen a client redownloading everything at every check...

> Did you just scan for tokens called "paperless*"

Yes, exactly that. As for why…

Paperless was absolutely hammering our server. The internal email thread about it began: "Every 10 minutes we see a massive outgoing network spike that's almost 3 times our normal bandwidth. What is going on there?"

Turned out paperless was downloading the entire contents of every single message in the account it's connected to (often GBs of data!) every 10 minutes. We run ludicrously powerful hardware and give ourselves capacity headroom so we could cope, but this was clearly broken behaviour and had the potential to impact other users. We added better per-user throttling to deal with it on our end, but also made sure that Paperless fixed this, and then wanted to ask people who looked like they might be using it to update. It will save you a ton of bandwidth and compute too.

While you are here, it was funny and a bit "scaring" at the same time to get your email about upgrading my installation of Paperless-ngx connected to my Fastmail account :)

Do you have any more insights on that one? Was it overloading the servers for no good reason I guess? Did you just scan for tokens called "paperless*" or did you use some extra heuristic?

children.author: thephyber
children.text:
This seems naive.

There have been several companies who admitted that they stopped using website chatbots, for example, because users were extremely creative with using it to hallucinate discounts, to leak internal documents, and generally to use it for free LLM output unrelated to the website. All of these would be considered "prompt injection".

You seem to care about some extremely high severity prompt injection. The Binance hackers used Binance's internal AI tool to describe the topology of the network and create a blueprint of sorts to identify how to extract the funds. It may not qualify as "prompt injection" in your mind, but a layer designed to resist malicious use (eg. Prompt injection) should probably have rejected those prompts.

This is something I'm increasingly curious about - we're a fair way in to mass corporate adoption of agents and AI (at least in tech) and yet the number of serious real-world security incidents traced to traced to prompt injection and adjacent problems, poor MCP security etc seems to be effectively zero.

The theoretical risk seems huge, and the 'payoff' the same impacts that drive aggressive and sophisticated ransomware etc campaigns so why is not clear. Maybe people are just keeping quiet but the tenor the security industry doesn't seem to be mapping to the real world in this case and why isn't clear.

The prospect of users trusting all their data to Google and risking to lose everything when Google unilaterally decide to close their account is chilling.

I've switched to other providers for everything (I no longer have a Google or Apple or Meta accounts, and I back everything up locally) and I sleep much better that way.

BTW, isn't that 4 months delay longer than the maximum allowed by GDPR? IIRC a recipient of a GDPR data access request has a maximum delay of 1 month to acknowledge it and request an extension, and has maximum 3 months to comply

Just in case: I once enabled SMTP access to my account because I had to contact a bunch of volunteers for an event and wanted to send personalized emails instead of "Dear volunteer". GMail flagged me as a spammer, banned my account, and it took four months and the GDPR to get it back.

So if you want to use SMTP but haven't done so until now I suggest you start enabling it to "warm up" their spam detector.

> [You may not] retain any user data obtained via GWS Access Tools or any Google Technical Information after you have disconnected the GWS Access Tool or revoked its access to the GWS Access Point(s);

N.b. this is for any access tool, not just AI.

This kills a whole bunch of products. No backup product can use the API, I can't connect my email to my accounting package and say 'please keep these receipts / documents safe for me' via the API.

"Google Technical Information" is essentially any derived information.

In essence your emails are no longer yours with this policy.
